Johnny Clegg - A Tribute

By: Diana Lucas | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
Johnny Clegg’s death on the 16th July of pancreatic cancer has South Africa in mourning from musicians, artists, music critics to the man in the street. His music bridged a gap and united South Africans. It would very hard to find someone who has not heard of Johnny Clegg, it’s been 40 years since he began his remarkable career wooing audiences locally and abroad with his uniquely South African sound.

We pay tribute and celebrate this extraordinary musician, writer, singer, performer talking to his fellow artists, friends and hopefully family.


Further information:
The people I will try and get are his dear friend and manager Roddy Quin, friend and artists Yvonne Chaka Chaka, Sipho Hotstix Mabuza, (who was playing The Crossing just before Clegg died) Ladysmith Black Mambazo; Abigail Kubeka; Vuysi Mahlasela, music guru Sean Brokensha. I will also try and interview his bandmate Sipho Mchunu who we interviewed in our programme.

We must try and interview his son, Jesse Clegg and his wife.

The French Consulate…because not only did they love this ‘Zoulou Blanc’ but he was awarded the ‘Chevalier des Arts et Lettres’ in 1991. He received the OBE from the UK government in 2015. He also received the order of Ikhananga from South Africa which is the highest hour a citizen can receive in South Africa.

He was not just an incredible musician but represents our past and the best of our future.
In the 70’s, mixed performances in public places were banned under apartheid. Juluka refused to step back and instead went under cover performing at universities, church halls, and even in the lounges of some people’s houses.

In 1986 Johhny wrote Asimbonanga honouring Mandela and other struggle heroes. In 1999 he performed the song (we saw you, we remember you…) when Mandela unexpectedly joined him on stage, a moment captured on film for millions of viewers worldwide.

He crossed colour lines and borders. South Africans are united in their love for him. He was able to unite us as a country.

Press Release:


Johnny Clegg – A Giant among Men
Carte Blanche pays tribute to legendary musician, songwriter and activist Johnny Clegg. Best known for some of his iconic hits such as ‘Impi’ and ‘Asimbonanga’ – a song paying homage to Nelson Mandela and other struggle stalwarts of his time – the man fondly known as the ‘White Zulu’ succumbed to pancreatic cancer earlier this week. As South Africa mourns the passing of yet another musical giant, we remember a man who embraced, comforted and fought for his compatriots, during a time in this country when it was dangerous to do so.
Producer: Diana Lucas
Presenter: Claire Mawisa


Script:


V/O
Johnny Clegg has left us… on Tuesday he passed away, after battling pancreatic cancer for four years.

Link: Son of the Johnny Clegg was our countries greatest cultural ambassador he personified what we envisaged what a united South Africa would look like re Johnny what he meant to us in South Africa and internationally

Sipho: So in life he left just as I knew him a good man. He was a strong person kind and caring. Now my heart is broken. Alas God knows.

V/O
Johnny Clegg’s first band Juluka, was a partnership with Sipho Mchunu, but the beginning of their friendship, goes back to when 16 year old Johnny was at school, and 17 year old Sipho, was working as a gardener.

Johnny
We were both lighties, 16 years old we went on a journey together of 15 years music was and expression of friendship and my interest in Zulu culture, our music was crossover we were trying to make a third thing of what had been separated.

V/O
It was Des and Dawn Lindberg who gave them their first break.

Sipho: They invite us to their house they were having a dinner, they said come to the house.
Claire: You go with Johnny tell us what happened
Sipho: I was very shy and Des said how are you feeling and I said no I’m okay. they give us wine old brown sherry to make us strong, warm. We ended up drinking, drunk so I said to Johnny how we going to play and he said you play, no you play and everybody, people thought we were acting.

Dawn Lindberg: He brought his whole Impi with him and he his his impis in the palm trees down the driveway and we gave the signal and the Impi’s started chanting and stamping and the neighbours phoned the police and said we think the riot has started at the Lindberg’s soirees.

V/O
On Johnny’s Final Tour Sipho came out of retirement and joined his friend on stage, taking them back to a different time to the early days of Juluka, when performing they had to go under cover.

Johnny I was arrested when I was 16 at Wemmer Hostel a male only hostel at the bottom of Rissik street that used to house 3 000 migrant workers we used to dance their on Sundays and their was a raid on the hostel by SAP and they couldn’t really see me and I was small, and it was two 2 constables and one looked at me and looked again and he had a shock and he came over to me and said what are you doing here
Johnny he thought I had been kidnapped or whatever…….so he took me to my mom because I was too young to be put into jail.

LINK
What made South African’s fall in love with Johnny Clegg was that he had a desire to represent our culture not just respectfully, but authentically as well.

Yvonne Chaka Chaka: He was just so amazing from that when I met Johnny Clegg we spoke in Isizulu, he never spoke to me in English He spoke perfect Zulu, he knew about idioms, he knew who he was and he knew what he wanted to be.

Sipho ‘Hotstix’ Mabuse: Johnny simulated his music into the pop genre of what was happening at the time so they were very unique. Johnny identified himself with the struggle of the African people and for that reason he was loved.

V/O
It was the international hit Scatterlings of Africa, released in 1983, that changed everything for Juluka.

Des He was a very effective activist because he never actually wrote down and out protest songs but he recorded what was happening in most beautiful form, harmony and choral singing and his own singing with Sipho and later Savuka and he got it down.

V/O
In 1985 Juluka split up.. Johnny formed another band Savuka with musician and dancer Dudu Ndlovo.….but in 1993 Dudu was killed in the political violence.

Johnny: Like every SA you know someone who paid the ultimate sacrifice and I think when Dudu was assassinated it took the breath out of Savuka.

V/O
And in memory of Dudu, Johnny wrote The Crossing.

Up Sound ‘The Crossing’.

V/O
In 1986 Johhny wrote Asimbonanga honouring Mandela and other struggle heroes.

Up Sound

V/O
Thirteen years later at a concert in Frankfurt, Germany

Johnny: I was singing the song and the crowd went OOOOOO
… and he was walking slowly on with Mandisa my singer, I am a song writer and for me that is the pinnacle of my song writing that song and that moment to have it validated by the man I wrote it for it was just the universe making these two things happen.

V/O
In 2015 when Johnny was diagnosed with cancer he decided he would say farewell to us, in the way he knew best…and embarked on The Final Tour.

Sipho: I was watching his moving dancing
Claire: Were you scared for him
Sipho: Very scared I didn’t show him Didn’t tell I was very worried

Yvonne He fought and he really conquered because he was strong, he never felt sorry for him self.

V/O 4/5 secs
We mourn with his wife, Jenny and their sons Jaron and Jesse.

Sipho We used to laugh a lot, that was the biggest thing laughing. His wife when she came in would say I knew Sipho was here and Johnny said Why…NO the way you laugh I know that Sipho was here.
Des: We lost a family member, and we wept.

Sipho ‘Hotstix’ Mabuse : You know its hard to imagine a world without Johnny Clegg
Its hard to imagine our country without a Hugh Masekela, Miriam Makeba, Nelson Mandela, We were a privileged country to have such people amongst us. And just to imagine that they are not going to be there, it’s unimaginable.
